newsitem.title: ARMENIA: Clampdown on opposition in Armenia after riots.
newsitem.headline: Clampdown on opposition in Armenia after riots.

text.p: President Levon Ter-Petrosyan called tanks and troops into Armenia's capital Yerevan on Thursday and arrested political opponents accused of trying to seize power by force in riots that followed a disputed presidential election.

In parliament, deputies voted overwhelmingly to strip opposition leader Vazgen Manukyan and seven of his supporters of their parliamentary immuntity, clearing the way for prosecutors to press criminal charges against them.
Manukyan, a former prime minister, was not in the chamber and his whereabouts were unknown. But the other seven deputies were led out of the hall by armed soldiers.
A prosecutor accused the deputies of trying to organise a coup d'etat and use violent means to seize power.
This correspondent saw armoured vehicles and several thousand troops with Kalashnikov automatic rifles sealing off the centre of the capital. Every pedestrian was stopped.
The clampdown followed violent clashes on Wednesday night between Manukyan's supporters, who accuse Ter-Petrosyan of rigging Sunday's presidential election, and riot police.
Police fired over the heads of a crowd of protesters. They hurled bricks and police waded in with truncheons.
An aide to Ter-Petrosyan told Reuters a soldier and a protestor had been killed in the clashes and dozens were hurt.
Taciturn security officers sealed off the two-storey building of Manukyan's headquarters.

Unofficial results showed Ter-Petrosyan, who has led Armenia since independence from the Soviet Union in 1991, won 52.09 percent of votes cast to 41.07 percent for Vazger Manukyan. But Manukyan's supporters say their man won.
Reuters Television producer Nino Ivanishvili witnessed a police raid on the headquarters of a small opposition party.

"Armed people in camouflage broke into the building. They were dragging people out and punching and kicking them," she said. She saw at least seven severely beaten men being dragged into a police van.
Ter-Petrosyan spoke on television early on Thursday.
"In accordance with the constitution, I announce that all meetings, demonstrations and gatherings are forbidden without our permission," he said.
"We will take other legal measures if needed. The provocateurs will be punished."
International observers said there had been many violations during the poll, but they stopped short of calling it unfair.
Manukyan, 50, served at various times as prime minister and defence minister under Ter-Petrosyan, a Soviet-era dissident.
Ter-Petrosyan had been widely expected to win the poll, but Manukyan came strongly from behind when several opposition groups withdrew their own candidates and rallied behind him.
The campaign was bitter. Manukyan promised to raise wages up to 10 fold, revive domestic industry and attract investment. He accused the president of allowing corruption.

Ter-Petrosyan called Manukyan "a populist" and warned Armenia's eight-year war with Azerbaijan over the territory of Nagorno-Karabakh could re-ignite. A ceasefire has frozen the conflict for over two years.

On Thursday, he was even more adamnant. "I warned you of the danger of fascism...I am not happy that my forecast came true so quickly... We won't allow the very existence of Armenia and Nagorno-Karabakh to be put at risk."
People in the streets of Yerevan appeared shocked by the developments and disillusioned with Ter-Petrosyan, once undisputed leader of the tiny Caucasus state.
"We will never trust him again after this" said a middle- aged woman, who said she voted for him in 1991.
